Specialists from the Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence (GUR/HUR) special unit “Group 13” struck a Russian K-300P Bastion-P coastal defense missile system in Crimea.
The Bastion-P can launch P-800 Oniks supersonic cruise missiles, which can engage both maritime and land targets, as well as 3M22 Zircon hypersonic missiles.
The “Group 13” operators also destroyed two fuel trucks and struck a command-and-staff vehicle belonging to Russian forces on the peninsula.
UAV operators of Ukraine’s 22nd Mechanized Brigade “Mykolaiv” destroyed a rare 2S43 Malva self-propelled howitzer near the border with Russia’s Belgorod Oblast.

The competition between strike systems and air defense/interceptor systems continues to evolve on both sides.
In response to Russia’s growing use of jet-powered Geran-4 loitering munitions and Geran-5/Banderol cruise missiles, Ukraine has begun developing jet-powered interceptor drones. The aim is to address a class of faster aerial threats that can be difficult for conventional propeller-driven interceptors to engage.
Ukraine has also used Bars jet-powered drones in at least one strike campaign against Moscow. Their numbers are still believed to be limited, with propeller-driven drones making up the majority of Ukraine’s long-range strike fleet.
This highlights a broader issue for Russia: the need to develop and deploy compact interceptor drones before faster targets become more widespread. The challenge is not simply intercepting them, but doing so economically. Traditional air-defense systems and MANPADS can engage such targets, but using them against relatively inexpensive strike drones can be difficult to justify economically.
One potentially relevant example comes from Iran. Several years ago, Iran developed and deployed the 358 missile, a specialized system intended to engage UAVs. It is a subsonic weapon with a reported speed of around 700 km/h, an infrared seeker, and a turbojet engine, with a claimed engagement range of up to 100 km. Its design reflects a different approach to countering relatively slow aerial targets, without relying on the speed and cost associated with conventional high-performance surface-to-air missiles.
The missile has demonstrated its effectiveness, having shot down a number of U.S. and Israeli UAVs.
This is not necessarily an argument for simply copying the 358. The more important point is anticipating what types of drones may be heading toward Russian cities in the future and developing an interceptor that is capable of engaging them while remaining cheaper than the strike systems it is designed to counter.

Equipment seized by the now-dissolved Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) from the Assad regime following its fall has been handed over to the Syrian government.
The equipment includes Tochka ballistic missile launchers, Shilka anti-aircraft systems, and 2K12 Kub air defense systems.

Based on the assessment and direction of Iran’s Aerospace Force Command Headquarters, a number of liquid-fueled ballistic missiles were transferred from the Isfahan missile base to the Kermanshah missile base in recent weeks for use in future operations.
This is not a routine redeployment. The move is a part of a deliberate plan, likely driven by operational and tactical considerations.
During the night, a Russian Su-35S multirole fighter shot down a Ukrainian UAV with an R-73 air-to-air missile while monitoring the airspace in support of the “Vostok” (East) Group of Forces.

Footage shows UAV operators from the Alexei Berest Battalion of the First Ukrainian Volunteer Spetsnaz Brigade destroying a Ukrainian T-64 tank, vehicles, and personnel on the Kramatorsk–Druzhkivka axis in Donetsk Oblast.
A HIMARS strike by Ukraine’s 45th Artillery Brigade destroyed a 9A316 launcher-loader vehicle from a Russian Buk-M1/M2 air defense system.
